chunk_findings.detail: The change contains no product-code line at all (the diff is tests-only), so the added test cannot be the fail-first regression test the change's own intent demands ("Write the regression test first and watch it FAIL on the unfixed code"). Check the pre-change revision (`git stash` the test edit and run `uv run pytest -q tests/test_hook_core.py -k pinned_session_start`): the test still passes green, because everything it asserts — that the *default* strategy renders an `(auto …)` marker and that `config --set schedule.parallel fixed` renders `(fixed)` instead — is pre-existing config→string behaviour that existed before this diff, and the test deliberately writes its own pin rather than depending on the edit to `test_the_session_start_alias_and_the_entry_point_print_the_same_brief`. The only genuine detector of B6983363359 is the `a[1] == b[1]` equality check in the sibling test, and that check remains load-dependent by construction (that is exactly why it had to be pinned); the new test's two substring assertions cannot substitute for it, since they constrain neither the value of `N` in the `parallel:` line nor any other host-derived token. Concretely: a later change that keeps the `(fixed)` label but still derives the number (or appends a load/mem figure) from the host leaves the new test green (`"(fixed)" in text and "(auto" not in text` both hold) while the same-brief test flakes again under load — i.e. the bug this change claims to close is not actually locked down. chunk_findings.detail: The new refusal gate at `ddflow/api/gates.py:626` keys entirely off `scope.needs_ci`, and `needs_ci` is not a fact about the scope — it is a substring test against the human-readable reason: `Scope("full", why, needs_ci="rerun ci" in why)`. Eligibility for "refuse instead of launching the suite" is therefore decided by prose. That the coupling is real and easy to break is demonstrated by this diff itself: four separate messages in `_ci_not_passed_here` (lines ~145, ~148, ~152, ~155) had to be reworded to contain the literal `rerun ci` — before this change they said "this gate runs the whole suite", and the flag would have been `False` for all of them. Concretely, the refusal set is decided by wording, not by condition: the branch at testscope.py:145 ("no ci gate in this item's pipeline runs the whole suite, so this gate runs it") is reached on the same code path, yields `scope.scope == "full"`, and does not contain `rerun ci`, so `needs_ci` stays `False` and `ddflow gate run <id> unit_tests` still starts `pytest tests/ -n 24` from an item gate — the behaviour the stated intent forbids ("never start the full suite from an item gate"). Because the flag and the gate that consumes it are coupled only by a string constant with no test or type expressing the invariant, any rewording of the remaining four messages (or any message assembled such that the phrase is paraphrased, e.g. "run ci again") silently restores bug B9de2a7dc3e: the refusal at gates.py:626 no longer fires and the 13k-test suite is launched unasked again.

chunk_findings.detail: The new flag is derived from pipeline membership (`needs_ci="ci" in G.pipeline_for(it, cfg)`), but it is attached to *every* non-empty reason returned by `_ci_not_passed_here` — including the reason `"no ci gate in this item's pipeline runs the whole suite, so this gate runs it"`. That reason is not about `ci` being absent from `it`'s pipeline; it is the case where a gate named `ci` *is* in the pipeline but does not itself cover the whole suite (that is precisely why the message is phrased about a ci gate "runs the whole suite", and why this module has to compare the ci gate's coverage with the gate under test at all — otherwise a partial `ci` tree would be used as a whole-suite anchor for the selection). In that configuration `"ci" in G.pipeline_for(it, cfg)` evaluates True, so `gates.py` takes the new refusal branch and returns `scope.why` verbatim: the user sees a refusal whose reason says `"...so this gate runs it"`, plus ineffective advice to rerun `ci`. Rerunning cannot clear it: whether the item's `ci` gate runs the whole suite is a static property of the item/config, so `_ci_not_passed_here` returns the same non-empty reason on every subsequent run, and `ddflow gate run <id> unit_tests` stays refused forever (the `ci` gate itself is not rescued by the `a {what} runs the whole suite` early return either, since it is not a full gate). Only `--force` gets past it. The flag should be set only for the reasons a rerun of `ci` actually clears (the state/tree-evidence reasons), e.g. by setting `needs_ci=True` inside those branches rather than wrapping every non-empty `why`.

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `"selected_tests" not in ev` is now vacuously true and no longer checks what it was written to check. In the refusal path `_run_unit_tests` returns the synthesized dict `{"scope_why": ..., "body": body}` (see the helper change at line 95), which by construction never contains a `selected_tests` key, so the clause can never fail regardless of what the gate actually returned. Before this diff the same clause ran against the real `body["evidence"]` returned by the CLI, so it could catch a gate that refused with exit 3 but still reported a selection. Given input "ci gate has no outcome" the test now passes even if the underlying JSON contained `evidence: {"selected_tests": [...]}`, because that payload is stashed under `ev["body"]` and never inspected. If the intent is to prove the item gate does not select tests when ci is stale, the check needs to be applied to `ev["body"]["evidence"]` (asserting it is absent/empty), not to the wrapper dict.

chunk_findings.detail:
The outcome is decided by whether `roborev show` happened to print anything, not by the verdict of the job that was waited on. Line 93 sets `text = ""` whenever `show` fails (`shown.error`/non-zero exit), and lines 96-98 then branch on `text.strip()`: any non-empty `show` output makes the run `findings`, and empty output makes it `unavailable`. Both directions are wrong for inputs the code itself anticipates:

- `roborev wait --job <id>` exits 1 on a FAIL verdict but also "on a job error" (the code's own comment on line 96). A job error whose `show` prints the diagnostic is therefore returned as `Result("findings", ...)` with exit 1 — the module's contract (lines 3-9 of the docstring) says a run that "could not run" must be exit 2 / `unavailable`, not a reported standards failure against the change. The gate records "the change failed review" for a host/queue fault.
- Conversely, a genuine FAIL whose `roborev show --job <id>` exits non-zero (job record pruned/rotated on the shared host, `show` incompatible with that job id, etc.) yields `text == ""`, so line 98 returns `unavailable` with `"roborev job N ended with no review (wait exit 1)"` — exactly the "no result" symptom this fix exists to eliminate, even though a result (FAIL) was produced and the wait's exit code said so. `wait_s` never timed out here, yet the gate is recorded as un-reviewed.

Input that demonstrates the first case: enqueue over `mb..HEAD`, job 17 then dies server-side; `roborev wait --job 17` exits 1 and `roborev show --job 17` prints the error text → `main` prints `standards: findings` and returns 1 (should be `standards: unavailable` / 2). Input for the second: `roborev wait --job 17` exits 1 (FAIL) and `roborev show --job 17` exits non-zero → `standards: unavailable -- roborev job 17 ended with no review` / 2, discarding the FAIL verdict.

chunk_findings.detail: `roborev wait` exit 1 is treated as "the review found issues" whenever `roborev show --job <id>` printed anything — but the code's own comment on that line states that `roborev wait` "exits 1 on a FAIL verdict **and on a job error**". The two cases are not distinguished: the branch keys the outcome solely on whether `shown.stdout` is non-empty, not on the job's verdict/status. Concretely, on the loaded shared host this fix targets, a roborev job that dies (daemon killed / OOM / worker error) makes `wait --job N` exit 1 and `show --job N` print the job record (its status/error text) with exit 0, so line 98 returns `Result("findings", "roborev wait exited 1", ...)`, i.e. `Result.exit == 1`. That contradicts the module's stated contract in the docstring — "Exit 0 reviewed clean, 1 findings, 2 could not run / no result in time (never a pass)" and "says WHY when it gives nothing" — because no review was produced at all: the caller will record the gate as *findings* (phantom review failures against the item under review) instead of `unavailable` with the job id and reason, and the reported reason ("roborev wait exited 1") hides that roborev errored. The errored-job case can be separated without guessing: inspect the `show` payload's status/verdict (or `show --json`) and require an actual FAIL verdict before mapping to `findings`, falling back to `unavailable` naming job `N` otherwise.

chunk_findings.detail: The status read is now the sole discriminator between a FAIL verdict and an error, and every way it can come back empty degrades a real review into `"unavailable"` — the exact symptom this bug is about. `_job_status` returns `""` whenever `proc.capture([exe, "list", "--json", "--limit", "100"], ...)` does not exit 0 (stdout is empty, `json.loads("[]")` matches nothing), whenever the job id is not among the newest 100 entries, or whenever roborev's successful terminal status is spelled anything other than the literal `"done"` (the only evidence for that literal is the fake the author wrote in the test). Concretely: a worktree whose installed roborev rejects `--limit`/`--json` (older or differing build) makes `list` exit non-zero → `status == ""` → `run()` returns `unavailable` with reason "ended in an unknown state", even though `text` (from `roborev show`) holds the FAIL review that the pre-change `if text.strip():` branch returned as `findings`. On the loaded shared host this fix targets, that turns a completed review back into "gate unavailable", i.e. the failure mode of B37468487fb is re-entered through a new door.

chunk_findings.detail: `status == "done"` is treated as proof that the non-zero exit of `roborev wait` was a FAIL verdict, so the run is reported as `findings` / exit 1. That inference is unsound. The code's own comment (line 110-111) says `wait` exits 1 "on a FAIL verdict AND on a job error", and the enclosing function takes a `wait_s` deadline, i.e. `wait` can also be killed/timed out while the *job keeps running* — exactly the shared-host situation of B37468487fb. If the wait process is killed at the deadline (non-zero return from `proc.capture`) and the queued job then completes *cleanly* before `_job_status` calls `roborev list`, the job record reads `done`, and the code returns `Result("findings", …)` with exit 1. A clean review is thus reported as findings and the standards gate fails. The pre-fix code at least consulted `show`'s text before calling it findings; the new code never looks at the verdict at all, only at whether the process exited non-zero. There is no way to distinguish "exited 1 because roborev said FAIL" from "exited 1 because we killed it and the job finished afterwards".

chunk_findings.detail: The outcome of a real FAIL is now gated on a *second* roborev invocation succeeding and returning parseable JSON containing this job id. Any of the failure modes that the loaded shared host makes likely collapses to `""`, which makes the wrapper report `unavailable` — the exact symptom this bug is about. Concretely: if `roborev list` times out (`proc.capture` returns no stdout → `"[]"`), or if its stdout is not a bare JSON array (e.g. a log/warning line before the array, so `json.loads` raises → `return ""`), or if the job id is not inside the newest 100 entries returned by the hard-coded `--limit 100`, then a job whose review text was successfully captured in `text` is still reported as `unavailable` with the reason "ended in an unknown state with no review", while `text` actually holds the review. The decision is deliberately independent of the review's content, so a single flaky/truncated listing call flips findings → unavailable for a genuine FAIL.
